person.name: Albert_Einstein
person.summary: Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist whose work on relativity, light quanta, and gravity transformed modern physics. A Swiss and later American citizen, he also used his public standing to advocate for peace, international cooperation, and nuclear arms control.

conclusion: Einstein transformed humanity's understanding of space, time, and gravity, then spent his final years confronting the moral consequences of scientific power. His legacy endures as both a triumph of imagination and a call to responsibility.

events.title: Birth in Ulm
events.description: Albert Einstein was born in Ulm, in the Kingdom of Württemberg, while his father was a partner in a bed-feather factory. He entered an assimilated German-Jewish middle-class household.

events.title: Studies in Aarau
events.description: After leaving the Munich gymnasium and joining his family in Italy, Einstein enrolled at the Aargau Cantonal School in Aarau to prepare for university. He lived with the Winteler family, formed a relationship with Marie Winteler, and completed the Swiss Matura with strong marks in science and mathematics.

images.caption: Einstein’s 1896 Aarau maturity examination certificate
images.creator: The authorities of the Canton of Aargau, Switzerland

events.title: Attends Zurich Polytechnic
events.description: In 1896, Einstein entered the teacher-training program in mathematics and physics at the Swiss Federal Polytechnic in Zurich. He studied alongside Mileva Marić, sometimes relying on classmates’ notes when he skipped lectures, and completed the program with a teaching diploma in 1900.
events.background:
The Polytechnic was not simply a physics department but a federal technical school intended to prepare specialist teachers. Its mathematically oriented teaching diploma qualified graduates in physics as well, yet the curriculum demanded sustained formal mathematical training. That requirement clashed with Einstein’s preference for theoretical problems and thought experiments over memorizing established material. His former classmate Marcel Grossmann became especially important as a careful recorder of the lectures Einstein neglected; the two men’s connection would later prove consequential when Einstein needed more advanced mathematics.

The class also exposed the limits imposed on women in technical education. Marić was the only woman in her year in mathematics and physics and attended the same lectures. She left for Heidelberg University as an auditor during the winter of 1897–98, then returned to Zurich in April 1898. Although she passed the first examination in 1899, she failed the final diploma examination the following year, with weak results in mathematics, especially function theory, and only a middling evaluation for her thesis. A second attempt in 1901 also failed. Her experience makes clear that access to the Polytechnic did not translate automatically into a professional scientific career.

One lasting irony of these years was Einstein’s impatience with the very mathematics he regarded as an obstacle to a problem-oriented physicist. When the problem of gravity later required tools for describing curved space, his own command of the subject was insufficient. Grossmann, by then a mathematics professor in Zurich, located the relevant work on Riemannian geometry and the tensor methods developed by Christoffel, Ricci, and Levi-Civita. Thus a student friendship and a set of lecture notes belonged to a longer intellectual chain. In the immediate term, the diploma did not secure an academic assistantship: applications to the Polytechnic and other universities were rejected, sending him toward temporary teaching work before the Bern patent office job.

events.title: Joins Bern Patent Office
events.description: In June 1902, Einstein began work in Bern as a technical expert, third class, at the Swiss Patent Office. Recommended by his friend Marcel Grossmann, the post gave him a stable income while he pursued scientific questions.

events.title: Marries Mileva Marić
events.description: Einstein and Mileva Marić married in a civil ceremony in Bern on January 6, 1903. They began married life while Einstein worked at the Swiss Patent Office.

events.title: Publishes Special Relativity
events.description: Working at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern, Einstein published “On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies” in 1905, the paper now known as [[special relativity]]. He acknowledged Michele Besso for valuable discussion of the problem.

event_class.title: On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies

special relativity.explanation: A theory that treats the laws of physics as the same for observers moving uniformly relative to one another, reshaping how modern physics relates space, time, motion, and light.

events.background:
Bern was not an academic refuge but the setting of a precarious early career. After failing to secure an assistantship at the Zurich Polytechnic or elsewhere, Einstein had obtained a permanent civil-service post as a technical expert, third class, on Marcel Grossmann’s recommendation in June 1902. He and Mileva Marić lived from October 1903 to May 1905 on the second floor of Kramgasse 49 in Bern’s old town, now the Einsteinhaus. Their son Hans Albert was born in 1904. Outside office hours, Einstein’s circle had included Maurice Solovine and Conrad Habicht in the informal “Olympia Academy,” whose meetings combined philosophy, mathematics, and scientific reading; the group’s regular meetings ended in 1904.

The work in 1905 was not an isolated leap in one subject. In March, Einstein completed a study of the photoelectric effect; in April, he finished a doctoral dissertation calculating the size of sugar molecules in solution and a value for the Avogadro constant; and in May he published an analysis of Brownian motion. The dissertation mattered because it supported the still-disputed atomic hypothesis, which leading figures including Wilhelm Ostwald and Ernst Mach had questioned. Alfred Kleiner and Heinrich Burkhardt at the University of Zurich accepted it quickly, though the journal editor Paul Drude demanded corrections to its numerical result, delaying formal completion of the doctorate until January 1906.

A further short follow-up in 1905, Is the Inertia of a Body Dependent upon Its Energy Content?, drew out the mass-energy relation later condensed into E = mc². The paper’s immediate reception did not turn its author into a celebrity: that came much later, after the 1919 eclipse observations were reported as favoring the prediction of his general theory of gravity. Still, the cluster of 1905 studies gave experimental physics several distinct targets—from molecular motion to light’s action on matter—and established the questions that occupied Einstein’s later work. His own route from this stage to gravity began in 1907 with the insight that a person in free fall does not feel their own weight; the mathematical tools required for that project would take years longer to assemble.

events.title: Leaves Patent Office
events.description: In 1909, Einstein became a lecturer in theoretical physics at the University of Zurich and soon an associate professor, leaving his position at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern.

events.title: Moves to Berlin
events.description: In April 1914, Einstein accepted positions in Berlin with the Prussian Academy of Sciences and the University of Berlin, attracted by the city’s strong scientific community. Mileva Marić and their sons joined him briefly, but after the couple’s separation, Marić returned with the children to Zurich in July.

events.title: Formulates General Relativity
events.description: In 1915, while working in Berlin, Einstein presented the final field equations of [[general relativity]] to the Prussian Academy of Sciences, completing his new theory of gravitation.

images.caption: Prussian Academy publication on general relativity
images.creator: Königlich Preussische Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin.

general relativity.explanation: Einstein's theory of gravity, in which matter and energy affect the geometry of spacetime; it extends Newtonian gravity in regimes of strong gravity or high precision.

events.background:
Berlin gave Einstein an unusually protected working position: as a paid member of the Prussian Academy of Sciences, he was free of regular teaching duties, while the city’s scientific network included Max Planck and other leading physicists. The problem, however, had followed him from his patent-office years. In 1907, a thought experiment about a person in free fall—someone who would not feel their own weight—had suggested an equivalence between acceleration and gravity. By 1911 he also recognized a hard limit on his earlier work: light speed could not remain constant under gravity, so special relativity applied only when gravity was absent.

The obstacle was as much mathematical as physical. Ordinary distance rules in flat Minkowski spacetime could not handle a world in which geometry itself varied from place to place. In 1912 Einstein turned to Marcel Grossmann, his former Zurich classmate, then a mathematics professor. Einstein asked him to see whether the library held a usable theory; Grossmann returned with the answer: Riemannian geometry. He also identified work by Bernhard Riemann, Elwin Christoffel, Gregorio Ricci, and Tullio Levi-Civita, whose methods supplied the needed tools—tensor analysis, Christoffel symbols, and covariant differentiation. Their 1913 Entwurf theory was an important attempt, but it was not yet the fully satisfactory formulation.

## A prediction to test

One early practical test concerned starlight passing the Sun. In a 1911 paper, using an older Huygens-style approach, Einstein had calculated a deflection of 0.83 arcseconds. The mature theory gave roughly 1.7 arcseconds instead. That difference made a solar eclipse a decisive opportunity: stars close to the darkened Sun’s edge could be photographed and their apparent positions compared with positions observed at other times. The later 1919 eclipse observations associated with Arthur Stanley Eddington found a result nearer the newer value than Newtonian corpuscular theory, turning an abstruse mathematical achievement into international news. Erwin Freundlich subsequently initiated Potsdam’s Einstein Tower, built from 1920 to 1924 to pursue further astronomical tests rather than merely commemorate its namesake.

events.title: Marries Elsa Einstein
events.description: After his divorce in February, Einstein married in Berlin on June 2, 1919. The marriage followed several years of personal closeness, and his new wife increasingly managed his household and public obligations as his health required attention.

events.title: Eclipse Confirms Relativity
events.description: British eclipse expeditions observed starlight near the Sun in 1919. Arthur Eddington's Príncipe expedition and the separate Sobral observations produced results reported as consistent with Einstein's prediction that gravity bends starlight. The London announcement brought Einstein international public attention.

locations.name_modern: Príncipe Island, São Tomé and Príncipe

images.caption: 1919 eclipse negative testing Einstein’s prediction
images.creator: F. W. Dyson, A. S. Eddington, and C. Davidson

events.background:
The eclipse result arrived in a Berlin already transformed by war and personal upheaval. Einstein had joined the Prussian Academy of Sciences in 1914 with a salaried post and no teaching obligation, a setting that gave him the time to finish his work on gravity. By 1917 he was director of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics. Yet he was also ill for much of 1917–20, living in the apartment of his cousin Elsa Löwenthal at Haberlandstrasse 5, and his mother, Pauline, was dying of cancer. The end of World War I also made contact with his sons in Switzerland difficult.

The stakes of the eclipse test were unusually exact. In a 1911 paper, before the final form of the theory, Einstein had estimated that rays from stars passing close to the Sun should be shifted by 0.83 arcseconds. The gravitational field equations later gave about 1.7 arcseconds instead. An eclipse made the measurement possible because the darkened sky revealed stars ordinarily drowned out by the Sun’s glare; their apparent positions near the Sun could then be compared with their usual positions. The issue was not simply whether gravity existed, but whether it altered the path of light by the larger amount required by a theory in which space and time are curved.

The sudden public response changed the practical conditions of Einstein’s career. Lectures that might once have been attended chiefly by specialists now drew audiences eager to see the newly famous scientist. The confirmation also encouraged a more permanent observational program: at Erwin Freundlich’s initiative, the Einstein Tower was built in Potsdam between 1920 and 1924. It was intended for astronomical observations that could subject the theory to further tests. The episode therefore made a difficult mathematical account of gravitation into an international public fact, while leaving its predictions open to continued measurement rather than treating one eclipse as the final word.

events.title: Receives Nobel Prize
events.description: The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Einstein on November 9, 1922, for his services to theoretical physics, especially his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect. Because he was traveling in Japan, German envoy Rudolf Nadolny accepted the prize on his behalf at the Stockholm ceremony on December 10, 1922.

images.caption: Einstein’s Nobel Prize certificate, presented in 1922
images.creator: Sofia Gisberg[1]

events.title: Settles in America
events.description: After Hitler's rise to power, Einstein, already abroad, did not return to Germany. In October 1933 he began work at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, and Elsa joined him in the United States.

images.caption: Albert Einstein House in Princeton, New Jersey
images.creator: Dmadeo

events.background:
The Institute for Advanced Study offered an unusual setting for a scientist accustomed to the prestige and pressures of Berlin: it was designed for sustained research rather than a conventional teaching load. Einstein’s European reputation made the appointment immediately consequential, but his position also marked a break with the network of the Prussian Academy of Sciences and the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics that had supported his work for nearly two decades. His Swiss citizenship, held since 1901, gave him a legal status separate from the German state; American citizenship would not follow until 1940.

Princeton became a household as well as an intellectual refuge. Elsa had long handled the practical burden created by his celebrity—correspondence, visitors, travel, and finances—and the couple eventually made a permanent home at 112 Mercer Street. Her health deteriorated soon afterward, and she died in Princeton in December 1936. The move also placed Einstein closer to American public life at a moment when events in Europe made his views on war, refugees, Jewish institutions, and international cooperation increasingly urgent.

The Institute did not turn Einstein into the head of a school in the ordinary university sense. He remained notably individual in his working habits, pursuing problems of gravitation and a unified field theory while physics increasingly concentrated on quantum mechanics. The contrast mattered: the relocation preserved for him the time and institutional independence to pursue long-running theoretical questions, but it also began the Princeton years in which a figure already known worldwide as a physicist became an unusually visible public intellectual. That later visibility would make his interventions on the dangers posed by Nazi Germany carry weight far beyond the scientific community.

events.title: Signs Roosevelt Letter
events.description: On August 2, 1939, at Cutchogue on Long Island, Albert Einstein signed a letter drafted by Leó Szilárd to President Franklin D. Roosevelt, warning that Nazi Germany might develop atomic weapons and urging U.S. support for uranium research.

images.caption: Einstein-Szilárd letter to President Roosevelt
images.creator: Written by Leó Szilárd and signed by Albert Einstein.

events.title: Founds Atomic Scientists Committee
events.description: Einstein and Leó Szilárd founded the Emergency Committee of Atomic Scientists in May 1946, with Einstein as its chairman. The group sought to warn the public about the dangers of nuclear weapons, promote the peaceful use of atomic energy, and advocate international control as a path toward world peace.
events.background:
The committee emerged from a bitter divide among the scientists connected to the Manhattan Project. In July 1945, 70 project scientists signed the Szilárd petition asking President Harry S. Truman not to use the atomic bomb on moral grounds. The new organization brought together people who had worked directly on the project and others who had been consulted on producing the first bomb. Its eight-member board paired Einstein with Harold C. Urey as vice-chairman and included Hans Bethe, Thorfin R. Hogness, Philip M. Morse, Linus Pauling, Szilárd, and Victor Weisskopf. The group’s immediate practical target was a $1 million fund for public education about civilian, national, and international control of atomic energy.

Its central argument was deliberately stark. Atomic bombs, the committee said, could be made cheaply and in large numbers, would become more destructive, and had no foreseeable military defense. Secrecy could not solve the problem because other nations could rediscover the necessary processes. In that view, an arms race would not create security: preparations for atomic war would damage the social order, while an actual war would bring the weapons into use and threaten civilization itself. International control of atomic energy, followed ultimately by the elimination of war, was therefore presented as the only solution.

## Building a public campaign

The committee was incorporated in New Jersey on August 6, 1946, and used private donations to support a network of educational organizations rather than keeping the campaign solely in its own hands. Recipients included the National Committee for Atomic Information, the Association of Scientists for Atomic Education, the Federation of American Scientists, and the Atomic Scientists of Chicago, which published the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. Members undertook lecture tours and issued promotional material, including one of the first films to depict what a full-scale nuclear war might look like. They also opposed development of the hydrogen bomb.

The campaign sought backing for the 1946 Baruch Plan, a proposal for international control of atomic bombs submitted to the United Nations. Although the United Nations Atomic Energy Commission passed it, the Soviet Union did not accept it. As international relations worsened and the commission failed in 1947, the committee concluded that public education was a long-term task unsuited to an emergency body. By the end of 1948, its original urgency had given way to a broader push for world federalism and a world government.

events.title: Death in Princeton
events.description: Einstein died at Princeton Hospital in Princeton, New Jersey, on April 18, 1955, at age 76.
